groups.instruction: Listen to the episode and choose the best answer to each question. Questions follow the recording.

options.label: A
options.text: Words for bright colours.

options.label: B
options.text: Words for unpleasant smells.

options.label: C

options.text: The smell of the ground after rain.

options.label: B
options.text: The smell of sweaty feet.

options.label: C
options.text: The smell of rotten eggs.

options.label: A
options.text: A newly painted wall.

options.label: B
options.text: A freshly opened packet of ground coffee.

options.label: C

questions.prompt: How do English speakers often describe a smell?

options.label: A
options.text: By giving its exact weight.

options.label: B
options.text: By using the same number for every smell.

options.label: C
options.text: By comparing it with a familiar object.

questions.prompt: What does the adjective "fragrant" usually mean?

options.label: A
options.text: Completely silent.

options.label: B
options.text: Very colourful.

options.label: C
options.text: Pleasant smelling.

questions.prompt: What do parents in the example do when a child talks about a smell?

options.label: A
options.text: Stop the conversation.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask the child to write a scientific report.

options.label: C
options.text: Always encourage a long discussion.

groups.heading: Advanced: Distinguish description from judgement
groups.instruction: Listen to the episode and choose the best answer to each question. Questions follow the recording.
groups.answerInstruction: Choose ONE answer: A, B or C.

questions.prompt: Why can a long list of words for bad smells give a misleading impression of precision?

options.label: A
options.text: Every word in the list describes a different chemical substance.

options.label: B
options.text: Many of those words communicate dislike rather than a distinct smell quality.

options.label: C
options.text: The words have no meaning to any English speaker.

questions.prompt: Why can two opposing descriptions of the same perfume both be true?

options.label: A
options.text: The perfume must have changed while the speakers were talking.

options.label: B
options.text: Neither person can actually smell the perfume.

options.label: C
options.text: They express different personal responses rather than an agreed smell category.

questions.prompt: What contrast does Neil draw with taste words such as sweet and salty?

options.label: A
options.text: They depend entirely on the colour of a food package.

options.label: B
options.text: They tend to communicate a shared idea more readily than the smell judgements discussed.

options.label: C
options.text: They are never used in everyday conversation.

questions.prompt: How is the scope of the findings about conversational habits qualified?

options.label: A
options.text: The presenters specify that the pattern is found in the UK at least.

options.label: B
options.text: The presenters say every culture has been tested with the same result.

options.label: C
options.text: The presenters restrict the finding to professional chefs only.

questions.prompt: How is the link between parenting and adult discussion of smells presented?

options.label: A
options.text: As a possible explanation, not as a fully demonstrated cause.

options.label: B
options.text: As proof that adults completely lose their sense of smell.

options.label: C
options.text: As a claim that all parents react in exactly the same way.

questions.prompt: What role does the example "musty" play in the discussion?

options.label: A
options.text: It proves that English has no words describing smell qualities.

options.label: B
options.text: It is another word for an individual's favourite sound.

options.label: C
options.text: It provides an exception: a word describing a particular smell quality.
